v.q: How does `HashMap` find the bucket for a key?
o: It spreads `hashCode()` and maps it to an array index
It compares the key with every stored entry in turn
It sorts the keys and then uses binary search
It converts the key to a string and indexes by its length
v.w: Index is derived from the hash (roughly `(n - 1) & hash`). Within the bucket, `equals()` picks the exact key.

v.q: What happens to the hash code when it is mapped to a bucket?
o: It is spread and reduced to an index
It is sent to the database
It is compared to every key
It is sorted
v.w: HashMap spreads the high bits into the low bits and masks the result to the table size.

v.q: Two different keys land in the same bucket. What is this called, and how is it handled?
o: A collision; entries chain in a list or tree inside the bucket
A conflict; the second key replaces the first one
An overflow; the map throws an exception
A mismatch; the map rehashes both keys forever
v.w: Since Java 8 a long chain (8 or more entries, table big enough) is converted to a red-black tree, so the worst case is O(log n).

v.q: Which statement about collisions in HashMap is NOT true?
o: The second key replaces the first one
Colliding keys share a bucket
Long chains become trees in Java 8+
equals tells the keys apart
v.w: Different keys in one bucket live side by side. A key replaces another only when it is equal.

v.q: You use a mutable object as a key and change a field used in `hashCode()` after inserting it. What happens on `get()`?
o: The lookup probably misses, because the entry sits in the old bucket
The map moves the entry to its new bucket on its own
The map throws `ConcurrentModificationException`
The lookup still works because the reference is the same
v.w: Keys should be effectively immutable, like `String`, `Integer` or records.

v.q: Which key is safe to use in a HashMap?
o: A String or an immutable value
A List that you keep changing
An object whose hashCode returns a changing field
An array
v.w: A key must keep its hash code while stored. Arrays use identity hashes and mutable keys get lost.

o: Equal objects must return the same hash code
Objects with the same hash code must be equal
Unequal objects must return different hash codes
`hashCode()` must return the object's memory address
v.w: Equal hashes with unequal objects are allowed (collisions). Equal objects with different hashes break the map.

v.q: Which statement about the equals and hashCode contract is NOT true?
o: Equal hash codes mean equal objects
Equal objects must have equal hash codes
hashCode must be consistent between calls
Overriding equals means overriding hashCode
v.w: Different objects may share a hash code. That is a collision, which is allowed.

o: When size passes capacity times the 0.75 load factor
As soon as any bucket holds more than one entry
Every time a new entry is added
Only when `rehash()` is called by hand
v.w: Resizing doubles the table and redistributes entries, which is costly. Pre-size the map when you know the entry count.

v.q: Which constructor argument avoids repeated resizing when you know you will store 1,000 entries?
o: The initial capacity
The key type
The hash function
The thread count
v.w: Capacity above size divided by the load factor means the table never has to grow.

v.q: Is `HashMap` safe for concurrent updates from several threads?
o: No; use `ConcurrentHashMap` or synchronise externally
Yes; every operation is locked inside the class
Yes, but only for read operations
Yes, provided the keys are all strings
v.w: Concurrent writes can lose entries or corrupt the structure. Reads during a write may also see inconsistent state.

v.q: Which map is the right choice when several threads update a shared map?
o: ConcurrentHashMap
LinkedHashMap
IdentityHashMap
WeakHashMap
v.w: The others are not thread-safe. ConcurrentHashMap lets threads read and update without a global lock.

v.q: What is the average time complexity of `get()` and `put()` in a well-distributed `HashMap`?
o: O(n)
O(log n) always
O(n log n)
v.w: Constant on average. A bad `hashCode()` that clusters keys degrades towards O(n) or O(log n) with tree bins.

v.q: Which operation is NOT O(1) on average in a well-distributed HashMap?
o: Iterating all entries
get(key)
put(key, value)
containsKey(key)
v.w: Iteration visits all entries, so it takes O(n).

v.q: What does `HashMap` do with a `null` key?
o: It allows one `null` key, kept in bucket 0
It throws `NullPointerException` at once
It ignores the call without any error
It stores the key in a separate sorted list
v.w: `HashMap` allows one `null` key and many `null` values. `ConcurrentHashMap` and `Hashtable` reject both.

v.q: Which map allows a null key?
o: HashMap
ConcurrentHashMap
Hashtable
TreeMap with natural order
v.w: HashMap allows one null key. The others throw NullPointerException.
